p.src: Baoyu left the Xiaoxiang Lodge and hurriedly asked Qiuwen, “What does Father want me for?” Qiuwen laughed. “He didn’t call for you. Sister Xiren sent me to fetch you, but I was afraid you wouldn’t come, so I tricked you.” Only then did Baoyu feel relieved. “You could simply have asked me to come. Why did you have to frighten me?” As he spoke, he returned to Happy Red Court. Xiren asked him, “Where have you been all this time?” “I was with Miss Lin,” Baoyu replied. “We began talking about Aunt Xue and Cousin Baochai, and I ended up staying there.” “What did you talk about?” Xiren asked. Baoyu recounted their exchange of Zen riddles. Xiren said, “You two really have no sense. It would be well enough to chat properly about everyday things or discuss a few lines of poetry, but why did you have to turn again to Zen riddles? You aren’t monks, after all.” “You don’t understand,” said Baoyu. “We have our own insight into Zen, and no one else can join in.” Xiren laughed. “You have turned Zen meditation on its head, and now you expect the rest of us to puzzle over your riddles too.” Baoyu said, “In the past I was young, and she was childish too. So whenever I spoke carelessly, she would become angry. Now I am more careful, and she no longer gets angry. It is only that she seldom comes here nowadays, while I have my studies. On the rare occasions when we meet, we seem almost like strangers.” “That is just as it should be,” said Xiren. You are both several years older now. How could you still behave as you did when you were children?” Baoyu nodded. “I know that too. But let us leave that aside for now. Tell me, has the Old Lady sent anyone over with a message?” “There was no message,” Xiren replied. Baoyu said, “The Old Lady must have forgotten. Isn’t tomorrow the first day of the eleventh month? Every year the Old Lady follows the old custom of holding a winter-banishing party, where everyone sits together drinking and laughing. I already asked for leave from school today, but now that no word has come, should I go tomorrow or not? If I go, I will have asked for leave for nothing; but if I do not, Father will call me lazy when he finds out.” Xiren said, “In my opinion, you should go. You have only just begun to make some progress in your studies, and already you want a rest. I think you ought to apply yourself more diligently. Yesterday I heard Her Ladyship say how well young Master Lan studies. Even after returning from school, he continues reading and writing essays on his own, and every night he works until after the fourth watch before going to bed. You are much older than he is and are his uncle besides. If you should fall behind him, the Old Lady will be angry again. You had better rise early and go tomorrow.”

p.src: Sheyue said, “In weather as cold as this, if he goes after already asking for leave, the school will say, ‘If that was what he meant to do, he should never have asked for leave. Clearly he lied to get a day off and shirk his work.’ In my opinion, he may as well take the whole day off. Even if the Old Lady has forgotten, can’t we hold our own winter-banishing party here? Wouldn’t it be pleasant to make merry for a while ourselves?” Xiren said, “Now that you have started this, Second Master will be even less willing to go.” Sheyue said, “I simply believe in enjoying each day as it comes. I am not like you, so eager for a good name that you make him toil for a month just to earn two extra taels of silver!” Xiren spat contemptuously. “You little hussy! We are discussing something serious, and here you come talking wild nonsense again.” “I am not talking nonsense,” said Sheyue. “I am saying it for your sake.” “For my sake how?” asked Xiren. Sheyue said, “When Second Master goes to school, you pout and pine for him, wishing he would come back just a little sooner so that you can talk and laugh together. Why pretend now that you do not care? I have seen it all.”

p.src: Xiren was just about to scold her when someone came from the Old Lady with a message: “The Old Lady says that Second Master need not go to school tomorrow. Tomorrow she has invited Aunt Xue over to cheer her up. The young ladies will probably all come too: Miss Shi, Miss Xing, and the Li girls have all been invited to some sort of winter gathering tomorrow.” Before he had heard her out, Baoyu cried delightedly, “Of course! Nothing pleases the Old Lady more. Now I have her open permission not to attend school tomorrow.” Xiren said no more. The maid returned. Baoyu had studied diligently for several days and could hardly wait to enjoy this day of leisure. Hearing that Aunt Xue was coming, he thought, “Cousin Baochai will surely come too.” Delighted, he said, “Let us go to sleep quickly and rise early tomorrow.” Nothing more occurred that night. Early the next morning, Baoyu duly went to pay his respects to the Old Lady and then to Jia Zheng and Lady Wang. He explained that the Old Lady had excused him from school that day. Jia Zheng said nothing, so Baoyu withdrew slowly; but after walking a few paces, he dashed like a wisp of smoke to Grandmother Jia’s apartments. No one else had arrived yet. Only Qiaojie had come with her nurse and several little maids from Xifeng’s quarters. After greeting the Old Lady, she said, “Mother sent me ahead to pay my respects and keep you company for a while. She will come as soon as she returns.” Grandmother Jia smiled. “What a good child! I rose early and have been waiting, but none of them has come. Only your second uncle is here.” The nurse said, “Miss, pay your respects to your second uncle.” Baoyu in turn asked, “How is my little darling?” Qiaojie said, “Last night I heard Mother say that she wanted to ask Second Uncle over for a talk.” “What about?” asked Baoyu. Qiaojie replied, “Mother said that although I had been learning characters from Nurse Li for several years, she did not know whether I really recognized them. I said I knew them all and would read them for her. But Mother said I was only pretending. She did not believe me and said that I played all day, so how could I know any characters? The characters do not seem difficult to me. Even The Classic of Filial Piety for Women is easy to read. Mother said I was deceiving her and wanted Second Uncle to go over them with me when you had time.” Grandmother Jia laughed on hearing this. “Good child, your mother cannot read, which is why she says you are deceiving her. Tomorrow, have your second uncle go through them for her, and then she will believe you.” Baoyu asked, “How many characters have you learned?” “More than three thousand,” Qiaojie replied. “I have read all of The Classic of Filial Piety for Women, and half a month ago I began Biographies of Exemplary Women.” Baoyu asked, “Do you understand what you read?

p.src: If you do not, I could explain it to you.” Grandmother Jia said, “As her uncle, you ought indeed to explain such things to your niece.” Baoyu began, “There is no need to discuss King Wen’s consort; I expect you know about her already. Then there was Queen Jiang, who removed her hairpin and awaited punishment; and Wuyan of Qi, who, though ugly, could bring peace and order to the state. They were among the able and virtuous consorts. Among the talented were Lady Cao, Ban Jieyu, Cai Wenji, Xie Daoyun, and others. Meng Guang wore a thornwood hairpin and homespun skirt; Bao Xuan’s wife carried a pitcher to draw water; Tao Kan’s mother cut off her hair to entertain a guest; and there was also the mother who drew characters in the sand with a reed to educate her son. These women did not disdain poverty. Among those who suffered hardship were Princess Lechang, whose broken mirror was made whole again, and Su Hui, whose palindrome moved the emperor. There were still more who were filial: Mulan took her father’s place in the army, and Cao E threw herself into the river to seek her father’s body. There are many such stories—too many for me to recount. The story of Lady Cao cutting off her nose with a knife comes from the state of Wei. There were even more women who preserved their chastity; those tales can only be told gradually. As for celebrated beauties, there were Wang Qiang, Xizi, Fansu, Xiaoman, Jiangxian, and others. There were fewer stories of jealousy, such as the shearing of a concubine’s hair, or of yearning, such as the tale of the Goddess of the Luo. Wenjun and Hongfu were, among women…” At this point Grandmother Jia interrupted: “That is enough. Say no more. You have told her so much—how could she possibly remember it all?” Qiaojie said, “Some of those Second Uncle just mentioned I have read about, and some I have not. When Second Uncle explained the ones I had read, I understood them much better.” Baoyu said, “Then you plainly do recognize the characters, and there is no need to test you further. I have to return to school tomorrow.” Qiaojie said, “Yesterday I also heard Mother say that Xiaohong, who now serves in our household, originally belonged to Second Uncle’s quarters. Mother took her away, but no one has yet been appointed in her place. Mother is thinking of assigning someone called Wu’er, from the Liu family, to replace her, but she does not know whether Second Uncle wants her.” Baoyu was even more delighted to hear this and said with a laugh, “How carefully you listen to your mother! She may appoint whomever she pleases. Why ask whether I want her or not?” Then he turned to Grandmother Jia and said with a smile, “Just look at our little darling—so pretty and so clever! I am afraid she will surpass Cousin Xifeng one day, and she can read besides.” Grandmother Jia said, “It is well for a girl to be able to read, but needlework and sewing are more important.” Qiaojie replied, “I am learning that from Nurse Liu too—things like embroidery and chain stitching. I cannot do them well yet, but I have learned to make a few stitches.” Grandmother Jia said, “A family like ours naturally need not depend on doing such work ourselves, but you must at least understand it, so that others cannot take advantage of you later.”

p.src: What, you may wonder, had made Baoyu so absent-minded? It was all because Liu Wu’er was to enter Happy Red Court. The first time, illness had prevented her from coming; the second time, Lady Wang had expelled Qingwen, after which no one dared select any girl with the least beauty. Later, when they went to the Wu Gui household to visit Qingwen, Wu’er accompanied her mother to take Qingwen some things. Baoyu saw her then and found her even more delicate and captivating than before. Now, fortunately, Xifeng had remembered her and proposed putting her in Xiaohong’s vacant place. This was joy beyond anything he had hoped for. That was why he sat there lost in thoughts of her.

It was all because Liu Wu’er was to enter Happy Red Court. The first time, illness had prevented her from coming; the second time, Lady Wang had expelled Qingwen, after which no one dared select any girl with the least beauty.

Later, when they went to the Wu Gui household to visit Qingwen, Wu’er accompanied her mother to take Qingwen some things. Baoyu saw her then and found her even more delicate and captivating than before.
Now, fortunately, Xifeng had remembered her and proposed putting her in Xiaohong’s vacant place. This was joy beyond anything he had hoped for.
That was why he sat there lost in thoughts of her.

p.src: Grandmother Jia waited for the others, but when they still had not come by this hour, she sent another maid to summon them. Presently Li Wan arrived with her sister, accompanied by Tanchun, Xichun, Shi Xiangyun, and Daiyu, and they all paid their respects to Grandmother Jia. Everyone exchanged greetings. Only Aunt Xue had not arrived, so Grandmother Jia sent someone to invite her as well. Sure enough, Aunt Xue came over with Baoqin. Baoyu paid his respects and inquired after their health. Only Baochai and Xing Xiuyan were nowhere to be seen. Daiyu therefore asked, “Why hasn't Sister Bao come?” Aunt Xue pretended that Baochai was unwell. Xing Xiuyan knew that Aunt Xue was present and therefore did not come. Though Baoyu was puzzled that Baochai had not come, Daiyu's arrival made him set aside his thoughts of Baochai for the time being. Before long, Ladies Xing and Wang arrived as well. When Xifeng heard that her mothers-in-law had arrived before her, she felt she could not lag behind. She therefore sent Ping'er ahead to apologize for her absence, saying that she had been just about to come when she developed a fever, but would be there shortly. Grandmother Jia said, “If she is unwell, she need not come. It is high time we had our meal.” The maids moved the braziers a little farther back and set two tables in a row before Grandmother Jia's couch, where everyone sat according to rank. After the meal, they once again gathered around the braziers and chatted idly; there is no need to dwell on it.

p.src: But why had Xifeng not come? At first, she felt embarrassed that she was later than Ladies Xing and Wang. Then Wang'er's wife came to report, “Someone has come from Miss Yingchun's place to pay her respects to you, madam. She says she has not called on the ladies above, but has come only to see you.” Xifeng was puzzled when she heard this and wondered what could have happened now. She had the woman brought in and asked, “Is the young mistress well at home?” The woman replied, “How could she be well? I was not actually sent by the young mistress. The truth is that Siqi's mother begged me to come and ask a favor of you, madam.” Xifeng said, “Siqi has already been dismissed. Why should she come to me for help?” The woman said, “Ever since Siqi left, she has wept from morning till night. Then one day her cousin suddenly returned. At the sight of him, her mother flew into a terrible rage, saying that he had ruined Siqi, and seized him to beat him. The young man did not dare utter a word. But when Siqi heard the commotion, she hurried out and brazenly said to her mother, ‘It was because of him that I was turned out, and I too hated him for being so heartless. But now that he has come back, if you mean to beat him, you may as well strangle me first.’ Her mother cursed her: ‘You shameless creature! What is it you mean to do?’ Siqi replied, ‘One woman is meant for one man. In a moment of weakness I fell into his snare, and from then on I belonged to him. I will never give myself to another man. I hated him for being such a coward. A man should answer for his own deeds—why did he run away? Even if he never returned for the rest of his life, I would remain unmarried for the rest of mine. If you tried to marry me to someone else, I was prepared to die. Now that he has come back today, ask him what he intends to do. If his heart has not changed, I shall kowtow to you and ask you to regard me as dead. Wherever he goes, I shall follow; even if we must live by begging, I will do so gladly.’ Her mother was beside herself with fury and cried and cursed, ‘You are my daughter, and I refuse to give you to him. What do you think you can do about it?’ Who could have known that the foolish creature Siqi would dash her head against the wall? She split her skull, blood poured out, and she died on the spot. Her mother wept and tried in vain to revive her, then demanded that the young man pay with his life. Her cousin said, ‘There is no need for any of you to be alarmed. I actually made my fortune away from home, and it was because I missed her that I returned. My heart has been true enough. If you do not believe me, just look.’ As he spoke, he drew a casket of gold, pearls, and jewelry from inside his coat. At the sight of it, her mother softened and said, ‘If you truly cared for her, why did you never say anything?’ Her nephew replied, ‘Women are fickle by nature. If I had said I was rich, she might have wanted me only for my money.

p.src: Now she has proved that she cared only for the man himself, and that is truly rare. I shall give you the gold and pearls, and go buy a coffin in which to lay her to rest.’ Siqi's mother accepted the valuables and, forgetting all about her daughter, let her nephew do as he wished. Little did she know that her nephew would have two coffins carried in. Go back and tell her that I shall speak to your Second Master and have Wang'er settle the matter for her.” After sending the woman away, Xifeng finally came over to Grandmother Jia's quarters. But no more of this.

p.src: Now, on this particular day, Jia Zheng was playing a game of Go with Zhan Guang. The overall position was nearly even, but the life or death of one corner group remained undecided, and they were fighting a ko over it. A young servant from the gate came in and reported, “Master Feng is outside and wishes to see you, sir.” “Show him in,” said Jia Zheng. The servant went out to invite him in, and Feng Ziying entered. Jia Zheng hurried forward to greet him. Feng Ziying entered and sat down in the study. Seeing that they were playing Go, he said, “Please carry on. I shall watch the game.” Zhan Guang laughed. “My poor play is hardly worth watching.” “You are too modest,” said Feng Ziying. “Please go on.” Jia Zheng asked, “Is there some business you wished to discuss?” “Nothing in particular,” replied Feng Ziying. Please keep playing, Uncle; I shall learn a few moves myself.” Jia Zheng said to Zhan Guang, “Master Feng is an old friend of ours. Since he has no pressing business, let us simply finish this game before we talk. Master Feng can watch from the side.” “Are you playing for stakes?” Feng Ziying asked. “We are,” said Zhan Guang. “Then a spectator ought not to interfere,” said Feng Ziying. “It does not matter if you do,” said Jia Zheng. “He has lost more than ten taels already, and in the end he will never pay them. We shall just make him host a feast for us later.” Zhan Guang laughed. “That would suit me very well.” Feng Ziying asked, “Are you and Master Zhan playing on even terms, Uncle?” Jia Zheng laughed. “We used to play even, and he lost. Now I give him two stones, and he still loses. He often wants to take back several moves as well, and grows angry if I refuse to let him.” Zhan Guang laughed too. “That is not true at all.” “Just watch and see,” said Jia Zheng. They finished the game amid talk and laughter. When they counted the score, Zhan Guang returned his handicap stones and had lost by seven points. Feng Ziying said, “In the end, this game was lost in the ko fight. You had fewer ko threats, Uncle, and that gave you the advantage.”

p.src: Jia Zheng turned to Feng Ziying and said, “Forgive me for keeping you waiting. Now let us talk.” Feng Ziying said, “It has been a long time since I last saw you, Uncle. I came partly to pay you a visit, and partly because an assistant prefect from Guangxi has come to the capital for an imperial audience, bringing four foreign-made objects that would be fit for tribute. One is a folding screen composed of twenty-four openwork panels, all carved from red sandalwood. The insets are not jade, to be sure, but exceptionally fine crystal glass, carved with landscapes, human figures, towers and terraces, flowers, birds, and other designs. Each panel bears fifty or sixty figures, all women in palace dress, and the piece is entitled Spring Dawn in the Han Palace. Their brows, eyes, mouths, and noses, down to their gestures and the folds of their robes, are carved with remarkable clarity and delicacy. The embellishment and composition are excellent throughout. I thought it would be just the thing for the main hall in your Prospect Garden. There is also a clock more than three feet high, with a little boy holding an hour tablet; whenever an hour arrives, he announces it. Inside it are little figures playing a ten-part ensemble. Those two objects are heavy and cumbersome, so I have not brought them here yet. But the two I have brought with me are rather intriguing.” He took out a brocade case he had beside him. It was wrapped in several layers of white brocade. When these were removed, the first thing revealed was a glass box containing a gold stand lined with bright-red crêpe silk, upon which rested a pearl the size of a longan, dazzlingly radiant. Feng Ziying said, “I am told this is called the Mother Pearl.” He then asked for a tray to be brought. Zhan Guang promptly brought over a black-lacquered tea tray and asked, “Will this do?” “That will do,” said Feng Ziying. He then drew a white silk packet from inside his robe, poured all the pearls it contained loosely onto the tray, placed the Mother Pearl in their midst, and set the tray on the table. They saw the little pearls roll round and round toward the great pearl. Presently they raised it aloft, and not a single pearl remained elsewhere: all of them had adhered to the great pearl. “That is extraordinary,” said Zhan Guang. Jia Zheng said, “Such a thing does exist. That is why it is called the Mother Pearl: it is truly the mother of pearls.” Feng Ziying turned to the young servant who had accompanied him and asked, “Where is the other box?” The servant hastened to present a rosewood box. When they opened it, they found that it was lined with tiger-patterned brocade, upon which lay a folded bundle of blue gauze. “What is this?” asked Zhan Guang. “This is called a merman-silk canopy,” replied Feng Ziying. When first taken from the box, the folded bundle was less than five inches long and no more than half an inch thick. Feng Ziying unfolded it layer by layer, and after some ten layers it had already outgrown the table.

p.src: Feng Ziying said, “As you can see, there are still two folds within. We would have to take it into a lofty room to spread it out completely. It is woven from merman silk. If hung in the main hall during hot weather, it will not admit a single fly or mosquito, and it is both light and translucent.” Jia Zheng said, “There is no need to open it all the way; I fear it will be troublesome to fold again.” Zhan Guang and Feng Ziying therefore folded it away again, layer by layer. Feng Ziying said, “These four objects are not excessively expensive. He will sell them for twenty thousand taels of silver. The Mother Pearl is ten thousand, the merman-silk canopy five thousand, and Spring Dawn in the Han Palace together with the chiming clock another five thousand.” “How could we possibly afford them?” said Jia Zheng. Feng Ziying said, “Your family is related to the imperial house. Surely the palace could find a use for them?” Jia Zheng said, “There are many things there that would be useful, but where are we to find so much silver? Let me have someone take these inside for the Old Lady to see.” “An excellent idea,” said Feng Ziying.

p.src: Jia Zheng had Jia Lian summoned and told him to take the two objects to the Old Lady. He also sent for Lady Xing, Lady Wang, and Xifeng to come and inspect them, and had both objects demonstrated in turn. Jia Lian said, “He has two other pieces: one is a folding screen, and the other is a musical clock. He wants twenty thousand taels for the pair.” Xifeng interjected, “The objects are certainly fine, but where are we to find so much spare money? We are not provincial governors obliged to procure tribute for the throne. I have thought for years that a family like ours ought to establish some secure foundations—sacrificial lands or a charitable estate, for instance—and acquire houses to tend the ancestral graves. Then, if our descendants fall upon hard times, they will still have something to rely on and will not be utterly ruined. That is my opinion, though I do not know what the Old Lady, the master, and the ladies may think. If the gentlemen outside wish to buy them, however, they may do as they please.” Grandmother Jia and the others all said, “There is good sense in what you say.” Jia Lian said, “Then let us return them. The master merely told me to show them to the Old Lady because they might be suitable for presentation at the Palace. Who said anything about buying them to keep at home? Before the Old Lady has even spoken, you pour out this great stream of dispiriting talk!”

p.src: With that, he carried the two objects out and reported to Jia Zheng that the Old Lady did not want them. Jia Zheng then said to Feng Ziying, “Fine as these two pieces are, we simply do not have the money. I shall keep watch for you, and if I find anyone who wants to buy them, I will send you word.” Feng Ziying had no choice but to pack them away. He sat chatting idly for a while, but, having lost his spirits, soon made to leave. Jia Zheng said, “Stay and have supper with me.” Feng Ziying replied, “No, thank you. Must I impose upon you merely because I happened to call, Uncle?” “What a thing to say!” said Jia Zheng. As they spoke, a servant announced, “The elder master has arrived.” Jia She had already entered. They exchanged greetings and polite inquiries. Before long, wine was served and the table spread with dishes, and they all began drinking. After four or five rounds, the talk turned to foreign goods. Feng Ziying said, “Such wares are hard to sell. Only a household like your honored mansion can afford them; elsewhere it is difficult.” “Not necessarily,” said Jia Zheng. Jia She said, “Our family is not what it once was. Nowadays we are little more than an empty façade.” Feng Ziying asked, “Is Master Zhen of the eastern mansion well? When I saw him the other day, we spoke of family matters, and he remarked that his son’s second wife was far inferior to the former young mistress, Lady Qin. I did not ask which family the new wife came from.” Jia Zheng replied, “Our grandnep’s wife also comes from a prominent local family. She is the daughter of Master Hu, formerly Intendant of the Metropolitan Region.” Ziying said, “I know Intendant Hu. But the discipline in his household leaves something to be desired. Still, no matter—so long as the young lady herself is good.”

p.src: Jia Lian said, “I hear from people at the Grand Secretariat that Jia Yucun is to be promoted again.” Jia Zheng said, “That would be good, though I do not know whether the report is reliable.” Jia Lian said, “It seems fairly likely.” Feng Ziying said, “I came from the Ministry of Personnel today and heard the same thing. Is the venerable Mr. Yucun a member of your honored clan?” “He is,” replied Jia Zheng. Feng Ziying asked, “Is the kinship close enough to require mourning, or more distant?” Jia Zheng replied, “It is a long story. His ancestral home is in Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, but he moved to Suzhou, where his fortunes were very poor. A man named Zhen Shiyin was his good friend and often gave him financial assistance. Later he passed the metropolitan examination, received an immediate appointment as county magistrate, and married a maid from the Zhen household. His present wife is not his original spouse. Who could have known that Zhen Shiyin would be reduced to utter destitution and disappear without a trace? After Yucun was dismissed from office, before he had any acquaintance with our family, my brother-in-law, Mr. Lin Ruhai, employed him as a private tutor while serving as Salt Censor at Yangzhou, and my niece became his pupil. When word came that he was to be reinstated and he needed to go to the capital, my niece happened to be coming here to visit her relatives. My brother-in-law Lin therefore entrusted her to his care and gave him a letter of recommendation asking me to put in a good word for him. He seemed a decent man then, and we often met. Strangely enough, Yucun knew everything about our hereditary line from the generation whose names contain the character Dai onward, as well as the members, residences, and domestic affairs of both the Ning and Rong mansions. Consequently, we came to feel quite close to him.” Then he added with a laugh, “After working the official backstairs for several years, he has learned how to advance himself. He was recommended for promotion from prefect to censor, and within only a few years rose to Vice Minister of Personnel and acting Minister of War. He was demoted three ranks over one affair, and now he is to be promoted again.” Feng Ziying said, “The rise and decline of men’s fortunes, and success or failure in official life, can never be predicted.” Jia Zheng said, “Yucun may count himself fortunate. Another family much like ours is the Zhen family. They once had the same distinguished service, the same hereditary privileges, and the same manner of life, and our two families were frequently in contact. Only a few years ago, when they came to the capital, they sent servants here to pay their respects, and the occasion was quite lively. Then suddenly their property in their native district was confiscated. To this day there has been no word from them. I do not know how they fare now, and I am truly concerned for them. When you see such things, can you imagine that officials feel no fear?” Jia She said, “Our family has the least cause for concern.” Feng Ziying said, “Indeed, your honored house has nothing to fear. First, you have the Imperial Consort’s protection within the Palace; second, you have many old friends and good relations; and third, from the Old Lady down to the young masters, not one member of your family is scheming or harsh.” Jia Zheng said, “We may not be scheming or harsh, but neither do we possess virtue or talent.”
